pages.title: Shock protection: Zs and the fault current
pages.for: An earth fault must open the device in time. Work Zs hot and keep it within the device's maximum. Then even at the lowest supply voltage, the fault current reaches the current that opens it.
pages.rule:
R1+R2 = mΩ/m × multiplier × L ÷ 1000
Zs = Ze + (R1+R2), or Zs at the board + (R1+R2)
Fault current = Uo × Cmin ÷ Zs, with Cmin 0.95
Maximum Zs = Uo × Cmin ÷ Ia
Pass: Zs ≤ maximum Zs, so fault current ≥ Ia
Longest run = (maximum Zs − Zs at the board) × 1000 ÷ (mΩ/m × multiplier)

On a 230 V TN supply: 0.4 s for final circuits to 32 A, or to 63 A with socket-outlets. Up to 5 s for distribution circuits and other final circuits. These are maximum times.
Too high? Bigger conductors or cpc, or a shorter run.
Or an RCD: then Zs need only meet Table 41.5, 1667 Ω at 30 mA.
Supplementary bonding where the time cannot be met.

traps.text: Leaving out the multiplier. The fault current then comes out bigger than it will be.
Using 230 V without Cmin, or with Cmax. Disconnection is judged at the lowest voltage.
Starting from Ze when the circuit is fed from a sub-board. Use Zs at that board.
Reading 0.4 s or 5 s as the time it will take. They are the longest allowed.
Working Zs out but never comparing it with the device's maximum.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: Zs = Ze + (R1+R2) must not exceed the device's maximum. Then the fault current opens it within 0.4 s for final circuits up to 32 A, or 5 s for distribution circuits.
pages.alt: The earlier lessons sized the circuit to carry its load. Now ask whether it disconnects on an earth fault. It must do so fast enough to protect anyone touching metalwork that has gone live. The fault current runs round a loop. It goes out on the line conductor, back on the cpc, and home through the supply. The loop's impedance is Zs = Ze + (R1+R2). The lower Zs is, the more current flows. Enough current opens the device within the time allowed. TIME ALLOWED On a 230 V TN supply, final circuits up to 32 A get 0.4 s. So do socket-outlet circuits up to 63 A.
pages.html:
The earlier lessons sized the circuit to carry its load. Now ask whether it disconnects on an earth fault. It must do so fast enough to protect anyone touching metalwork that has gone live.

The fault current runs round a loop. It goes out on the line conductor, back on the cpc, and home through the supply. The loop's impedance is Zs = Ze + (R1+R2). The lower Zs is, the more current flows. Enough current opens the device within the time allowed.

Time allowed

On a 230 V TN supply, final circuits up to 32 A get 0.4 s. So do socket-outlet circuits up to 63 A. Distribution circuits and other final circuits get up to 5 s. These are the longest times allowed, not how long it will take.

If it is skipped: A Zs over the device's maximum goes unnoticed. The fault current is then too small to be sure of opening the device in time.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: At 11.4 m, Zs is 0.366 Ω and the fault current 596.99 A. Near 37.9 m, Zs reaches 0.87 Ω and the current falls to about 250 A. At 50 m, 4 mm² brings Zs back to 0.740 Ω.
pages.alt: Fault current 750 A and up 0 A Ia, 250 A Within 0.1 s May trip Thermal: slow DBP2 Line out (R1) Fault at the starter Supply side 0.15 Ω cpc back (R2) Worked hot, × 1.28 The loop is 0.366 Ω, within 0.87 Ω, so 596.99 A flows at the lowest supply voltage. That is more than the 250 A that opens the breaker within 0.1 s. R1+R2 = mΩ/m × multiplier × length ÷ 1000 14.82 × 1.28 × 11.4 ÷ 1000 0.216 Ω Zs = Zs at DBP2 + R1+R2 0.15 + 0.216, within 0.87 Ω 0.366 Ω Fault current = 230 × Cmin ÷ Zs 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.366 596.99 A The limit is 0.87 Ω, the 25 A type C's maximum Zs.
pages.html:
The loop is 0.366 Ω, within 0.87 Ω, so 596.99 A flows at the lowest supply voltage. That is more than the 250 A that opens the breaker within 0.1 s.

R1+R2 = mΩ/m × multiplier × length ÷ 100014.82 × 1.28 × 11.4 ÷ 10000.216 Ω
Zs = Zs at DBP2 + R1+R20.15 + 0.216, within 0.87 Ω0.366 Ω
Fault current = 230 × Cmin ÷ Zs230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.366596.99 A

The limit is 0.87 Ω, the 25 A type C's maximum Zs. It comes from 230 × 0.95 ÷ 250 = 0.874 Ω, printed as 0.87.

A type C breaker trips instantly somewhere between 5 and 10 times its rating, so 125 to 250 A here. Below that, only its slower thermal part works. Take Ia as 250 A, the top of the band. That is the worst case, and the maximum Zs tables use it too.

Each metre adds resistance to the loop. A conductor that has been carrying current is warm, and warm copper has more resistance. The multiplier allows for that. The loop sets how much current the supply can push at its lowest voltage. The breaker is sure to open in time only once that current reaches Ia.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: Compare the hot figure, 0.909 Ω, with 0.87 Ω. At 40 m the run fails.
pages.answer: 0.909 Ω: the limit assumes conductors at working temperature
pages.alt: The milliohm figures are for copper at 20 °C. The maximum Zs values assume conductors at working temperature. The multiplier brings R1+R2 up to that.

Either: the gap is only rounding
pages.html: The milliohm figures are for copper at 20 °C. The maximum Zs values assume conductors at working temperature. The multiplier brings R1+R2 up to that.

pages.name: When Zs is too high
pages.text: At 50 m, Zs is 1.098 Ω and fails. 4 mm² brings it to 0.740 Ω. An RCD needs far less earth path. Supplementary bonding is the route where the time cannot be met.
pages.alt: Bring R1+R2 down. Use bigger conductors, a bigger cpc or a shorter run. A 4 mm² line and cpc gives 0.740 Ω. Use a breaker that trips instantly on less current. A type B does so at 3 to 5 times In, so its maximum Zs is higher. For a 25 A type B the rule gives 230 × 0.95 ÷ 125 = 1.748 Ω. On a job, read the real figure from Table 41.3. A type B does not suit this motor, though. In lesson 3 we chose type C so it rides through the starting current. Add an RCD for fault protection. It trips when line and neutral differ by its rating, 30 mA say.
pages.html:
Bring R1+R2 down. Use bigger conductors, a bigger cpc or a shorter run. A 4 mm² line and cpc gives 0.740 Ω.

Use a breaker that trips instantly on less current. A type B does so at 3 to 5 times In, so its maximum Zs is higher. For a 25 A type B the rule gives 230 × 0.95 ÷ 125 = 1.748 Ω. On a job, read the real figure from Table 41.3. A type B does not suit this motor, though. In lesson 3 we chose type C so it rides through the starting current.

Add an RCD for fault protection. It trips when line and neutral differ by its rating, 30 mA say. So even a poor earth path lets enough current flow to trip it. Table 41.5 allows 1667 Ω for 30 mA and 500 Ω for 100 mA.

Where the time cannot be met at all, add supplementary protective equipotential bonding.

Debated

The regulations point to this bonding when the times cannot be met. Some engineers argue it does not hold the touch voltage to 50 V in every fault.

pages.name: Section B (1)
pages.task: Explain why the factor Cmin is applied to the nominal voltage to earth when an earth fault current is worked out.
pages.why: A model answer: The supply voltage is not fixed. It can fall below the nominal 230 V, as low as 218.5 V. Cmin is the factor that allows for that. For a low voltage supply under the ESQCR, it is 0.95. The fault current is Uo × Cmin ÷ Zs. So a lower voltage pushes less current through the same loop. The device is sure to open in time only if that current reaches its Ia. So the design checks the smallest current the supply could give. If the device opens on that, it opens on anything higher. That is why maximum Zs values are worked at Cmin. For a 6 A type B breaker, 230 × 0.95 ÷ 30 A gives 7.28 Ω.

pages.name: Section B (2)
pages.task: State what a designer must consider for the showroom's EV charging points on its TN-C-S supply.
pages.why: A model answer: The circuit to the charging equipment must not include a PEN conductor. A PME earth must not serve an outdoor charge point on its own. One of three measures must hold the open-PEN voltage within 70 V. They are well-balanced loading across the phases, an added earth electrode, or a device that detects the fault. Making the point TT takes it off the PME earth altogether. An RCD is no protection against that fault. The load current goes out on the line and back on the neutral through it, so it sees no imbalance. PEN fault protection has to be designed in. Each charging point needs RCD protection, including protection against DC fault currents over 6 mA. That means a Type B RCD, or a Type A or F RCD with a detecting device, unless the charger provides it. Load management can be added to bring the maximum demand down, but it is optional. Section 722 has changed in recent amendments. Check it against the amendment you work to.
